```{r}
#| warning: false
# Plot A
h_5 <- function(x){
  x + 2
}
h_6 <- function(x){
  x + 4
}
curve(expr = h_5,
      from = 0,
      to = 12,
      xlab = "t",
      ylab = "h(t)",
      main = "Plot A")
curve(expr = h_6,
      add = TRUE,
      lty = 2)
grid()

# Plot B
cll_3 <- function(x){
  2 * log(x) - 2 * log(2)
}
cll_4 <- function(x){
  2 * log(x) - 2 * log(2) - 1
}
curve(expr = cll_3,
      from = 2,
      to = 12,
      xlab = "t",
      ylab = "log(-log(S(t)))",
      main = "Plot B",
      ylim = c(cll_4(2),
               cll_3(12)))
curve(expr = cll_4,
      add = TRUE,
      lty = 2)
grid()

# Plot C
h_3 <- function(x){
  sin(x / 8 * 2 * pi) + x
}
h_4 <- function(x){
  h_3(x) / 2
}
curve(expr = h_3,
      from = 0,
      to = 12,
      xlab = "t",
      ylab = "h(t)",
      main = "Plot C")
curve(expr = h_4,
      add = TRUE,
      lty = 2)
grid()

h_1 <- function(x){
  12 - x
}
h_2 <- function(x){

}
curve(expr = h_1,
      from = 0,
      to = 12,
      xlab = "t",
      ylab = "h(t)",

curve(expr = h_2,

grid()

# Plot E
cll_1 <- function(x){

}

}
curve(expr = cll_1,
      from = 0,
      to = 12,
      xlab = "t",
      ylab = "log(-log(S(t)))",
      main = "Plot E")
curve(expr = cll_2,
      add = TRUE,

grid()

# Plot F
S_1 <- function(x){
  -(x - 6)^3 / 432 + 1 / 2
}
S_2 <- function(x){
  1 - x / 12
}
curve(expr = S_1,
      from = 0,
      to = 12,
      xlab = "t",
      ylab = "S(t)",

curve(expr = S_2,
      add = TRUE,

grid()
```

## Problem 1

Each of the plots above shows two curves,
one for each group in a randomized controlled trial.
For each plot,
identify whether the proportional hazards assumption is met.
Each is worth one point.

### Part (a)


Plot A


(i) Proportional hazards assumption is met.
(ii) Proportional hazards assumption is not met.



::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

ii

The hazard functions are parallel, not proportional.

:::

### Part (b)


Plot B


(i) Proportional hazards assumption is met.
(ii) Proportional hazards assumption is not met.



::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

i

The complementary log-log functions are parallel.

:::

### Part (c)


Plot C


(i) Proportional hazards assumption is met.
(ii) Proportional hazards assumption is not met.



::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

i

The solid hazard function is twice the dashed hazard function.

:::

### Part (d)


Plot D


(i) Proportional hazards assumption is met.
(ii) Proportional hazards assumption is not met.



::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

i

The solid hazard function is twice the dashed hazard function.

:::

### Part (e)


Plot E


(i) Proportional hazards assumption is met.
(ii) Proportional hazards assumption is not met.



::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

ii

The complementary log-log functions intersect,
so they cannot be parallel.

:::

### Part (f)


Plot F


(i) Proportional hazards assumption is met.
(ii) Proportional hazards assumption is not met.



::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

ii

The survival functions cross, meaning $S_2(t) \ne S_1(t)^c$.

:::
        


## Problem 2


Please identify each of the following statements as true or false.
Each problem is worth one point.

### Part (a)

Cox regression estimates hazard rates.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

False.

Cox regression estimates hazard ratios.

:::

### Part (b)

The raw estimates of coefficients in logistic regression represent odds ratios,
and therefore cannot be negative.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

False.

The raw estimate of the intercept is a log odds and the raw estimate
of a slope is a log odds ratio.
Both of these can be negative.

:::

### Part (c)

I've developed a new blood test for a previously difficult-to-identify cancer.
The test has high sensitivity.
This means that if someone has the cancer,
they have a high probability of testing positive.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

True.

:::


### Part (d)

I've developed a new blood test for a previously difficult-to-identify cancer.
The test has high specificity.
This means that if someone tests negative,
they have a low probability of having the cancer.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

False.

High specificity means that if someone does not have the cancer,
they have a high probability of testing negative.

:::


### Part (e)

We can only compute $R^2$ for normally-distributed data.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

False.

:::

### Part (f)

Suppose you have a normally-distributed vulnerability index ($V_i$)
that you hypothesize has a different mean depending on race ($R_i$).
It doesn't make sense to write the linear model equation as
$E(V_i|R_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 R_i$
because $R_i$ is a categorical variable, not a numeric variable.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

True.

We would have to turn race into dummy variables in order to write down
a linear model that makes sense.

:::
